newsitem.title: FRANCE: Polisario frees Moroccan prisoners as Baker arrives.
newsitem.headline: Polisario frees Moroccan prisoners as Baker arrives.

text.p: The Polisario Front on Sunday freed 85 Moroccan war prisoners as U.N. envoy James Baker arrived at the Front's base in Algeria to discuss the future of the disputed Western Sahara, Algerian state radio reported.

The radio said Polisario leader Mohamed Abdelaziz took the decision to free the prisoners as a goodwill gesture to help Baker break an impasse in a U.N. peace plan for the territory largely controlled by Morocco.

Baker arrived earlier in the southwestern Algerian town of Tindouf, Polisario's main rear base and headquarters of its self-declared Saharan Arab Democractic Republic (RASD) government, as part of a regional tour.
The Algerian official news agency APS said Baker began talks with Abdelaziz, who is also president of the RASD which is recognised by about 70 countries.

The former U.S. secretary of state will hold a news conference in Tindouf later on Sunday over his visit to tackle the dispute over the control of the former Spanish colony which has gone on for more than 20 years, APS said.
Baker, who arrived from Mauritania, is on his first trip to the region since U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed him his personal envoy for Western Sahara last month.
He has also visited Morocco and held talks with Algerian leaders in Algiers on what he terms a "fact-finding" mission.

APS said Baker would also visit refugee camps in Tindouf, home to thousands who fled years of conflict in Western Sahara before a U.N. ceasefire in September 1991 ended fighting between the Polisario and Moroccan troops.

The second part of a U.N. peace plan, a referendum to enable Saharans to decide whether the territory should be independent or integrate with Morocco, has been held up by disputes over who should be allowed to vote.
The ballot was initially planned for January 1992.
APS earlier on Sunday quoted Polisario foreign minister Bachir Mustapha Sayed as telling reporters in Tindouf that Baker faced a "great challenge" over the U.N. peace plan.
But Baker's diplomatic experience, political weight and his backing by the Security Council and international community would enable him to answer the challenge, Mustapha Sayed said.
